summary: Defines a YANG data model and mechanisms that let a subscriber ask a publisher for a customized, continuous stream of events. A subscriber can set up subscriptions so it receives only the information it wants, as generated by the publisher.

eli5.summary: It is like signing up for text alerts about just the topics you care about, instead of getting every message from the whole school.

questions: how to subscribe to yang events
what is a yang event stream
subtitle: A transport-independent way to subscribe to a device's event streams and get a customized, continuous feed.

tldr.problem: Earlier NETCONF notification subscriptions (RFC 5277) were tied to NETCONF and limited: one subscription per session, no changes in flight, no per-subscription counters.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG data model and RPCs let a subscriber establish, modify, delete or kill dynamic subscriptions to named event streams, with filters, QoS, replay and stop times. Configured subscriptions can instead be installed through configuration, and the publisher reports changes with subscription state change notifications.
tldr.outcome: A publisher can push filtered event records to receivers over any transport that meets the stated requirements, with bindings for NETCONF and RESTCONF defined elsewhere.

today: RFC 8639 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2019. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is used together with RFC 8640 for NETCONF delivery and RFC 8641 for datastore updates.

sections.title: The Problem and the Big Idea
sections.content:
This RFC defines a YANG data model and mechanisms for subscriber-specific subscriptions to a publisher's event streams. It gives a 'subscribe, then publish' capability: the publisher knows what each receiver wants and is allowed to see before it packages and pushes event records. The functionality is transport agnostic; NETCONF or RESTCONF can configure or signal subscriptions, and their delivery bindings are defined in RFC 8640 and a separate RESTCONF document.

It builds on earlier work: limits of the RFC 5277 subscriptions were partly addressed by the requirements in RFC 7923. The goals are multiple subscriptions on one transport session, dynamic and configured subscriptions, modifying a subscription in progress, per-subscription counters, negotiation through hints in declined requests, state change notifications and independence from transport.
sections.eli5: Instead of a device shouting every event at everyone, you tell it exactly which kinds of news you want and it only sends you those.

sections.title: Event Streams, Filters and QoS
sections.content:
An event stream is a named entity on a publisher that exposes a continuously updating set of YANG-defined event records. Only one stream name is reserved, NETCONF; implementations MAY define more. Event records MUST NOT be delivered to a receiver in a different order than they were placed on the stream. Access control may silently exclude records a receiver may not read.

A filter is a boolean test on an event record. A false result excludes the record, and a filter never strips information from a record. Two optional syntaxes are supported: XPath and subtree. With no filter, all records on the stream are sent.

Quality of service parameters treat a subscription relative to other traffic: a dscp marking, a weighting for proportional bandwidth, and a dependency on another subscription. Weighting and dependency only apply between subscriptions sharing the same dscp value, and are advertised through the qos feature.
sections.eli5: A stream is like a TV channel. A filter is a rule such as 'only show me the cartoons', and the priority settings decide whose show gets sent first when the line is busy.

sections.title: Dynamic Subscriptions
sections.content:
A dynamic subscription is created by the subscriber with an RPC and lives only as long as the transport session that created it. Four RPCs manage it: establish-subscription, modify-subscription, delete-subscription and kill-subscription. The last lets an operator end a dynamic subscription that belongs to a different session.

Establishing takes a stream name, an optional filter, an optional encoding, an optional stop-time and an optional replay-start-time. If the publisher accepts, it replies with a subscription identifier and starts streaming. A rejected request may carry hints in a yang-data error container describing parameters that might succeed. A failed modify leaves the subscription exactly as it was.

With replay, the subscription first sends logged records from after replay-start-time (and before any stop-time), then a replay-completed notification, then new records. If the requested start is earlier than the log holds, the publisher reports its revised time in replay-start-time-revision.

A publisher may suspend a subscription when CPU or bandwidth is short. A suspended subscription returns to active when modified successfully or when resources return.
sections.eli5: You walk up and ask the device, 'please send me these news items.' You can change your mind later, ask it to replay what you missed, or tell it to stop.

sections.title: Configured Subscriptions
sections.content:
A configured subscription is installed through configuration into the top-level subscriptions subtree. It survives publisher reboots, survives when no transport is available, and can send to more than one receiver, none of which know about the others. Support is optional on the publisher and advertised with the configured feature. It adds parameters such as a transport, one or more receivers and optional egress choices: source-interface, source-address and source-vrf.

The publisher evaluates a configured subscription as valid, invalid or concluded. Each receiver of a valid subscription moves among connecting, active, suspended and disconnected. A receiver becomes active when a subscription-started notification is delivered. If it cannot be served because of buffer limits or insufficient CPU, it becomes suspended.

A reset action on a receiver forces a new connection attempt and a new subscription-started. Configured replay sends the records buffered since the last publisher restart. Dynamic and configured operations are not mixed: RPCs cannot modify a configured subscription, and configuration cannot directly modify a dynamic one.
sections.eli5: A configured subscription is like a standing newspaper delivery. It keeps coming even after a power cut, and the paper can go to several houses.

sections.title: Notification Messages and State Changes
sections.content:
Event records are delivered in notification messages. Each MUST include an <eventTime> element at the top level, as shown in RFC 5277. After an establish or modify RPC, matching records MUST NOT be sent until the RPC reply has been sent.

The publisher MUST also send subscription state change notifications. They are never part of an event stream, cannot be dropped or filtered, are not stored in replay buffers, and go only to affected receivers. They are:

  • subscription-started: a configured subscription began; never sent for dynamic ones.
  • subscription-modified: parameters changed, including when a referenced filter changed.
  • subscription-terminated: no more records should be expected, with a reason such as filter-unavailable, stream-unavailable or suspension-timeout.
  • subscription-suspended: with reason insufficient-resources or unsupportable-volume.
  • subscription-resumed, subscription-completed (stop time reached) and replay-completed.

Operators can monitor state through the subscriptions container, which has per-receiver counters sent-event-records and excluded-event-records.
sections.eli5: Besides the news itself, the device sends little notes such as 'your delivery started', 'your delivery is paused' or 'your delivery has ended'.

sections.title: Transport Requirements
sections.content:
Because the design is transport independent, the RFC lists what a transport must provide. It MUST support multiple establish-subscription requests in one session. The publisher MUST authenticate a receiver at the transport level before sending event records, and the receiver MUST authenticate the publisher, giving mutual authentication. A secure transport is highly recommended, and the publisher MUST check that the receiver is authorized for the content involved.

Event records and subscription state change notifications MUST be sent on the same transport session so delivery stays ordered. A transport specification MUST list its supported encodings and, for configured subscriptions, the default encoding. A publisher supporting configured MUST support at least one model that augments transport connection parameters onto each receiver.
sections.eli5: The delivery truck can be any kind, but both sides must prove who they are, and the packages must arrive in the order they were sent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The model is accessed over NETCONF or RESTCONF. Access can be restricted with the Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341). Notifications SHOULD NOT be sent to a receiver that does not support this specification, since configured subscriptions could be used to overwhelm a receiver.

Many risks are about resources: a large number of establish-subscription requests, complex filters, big replays, or a large weighting. Publishers MUST reject requests they lack resources for, and kill-subscription MUST be limited to connections with administrative rights. Replay can expose historical data to subscribers who were not authorized when it was collected, and a publisher with a wrong clock can cause replays or lost messages.
sections.eli5: Because anyone could ask for lots of deliveries and clog the system, the device checks who is asking and refuses requests it cannot handle.
